lessons.title: Beginning with "Read"
lessons.objective: Examine Surah al-'Alaq 96:1 as the Qur'an's opening call to read in the name of the Creator.
lessons.hook: Why is it striking that the first revealed word of the Qur'an is an invitation to read?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: Read in the Name of your Lord who created;

lessons.summary: Surah al-'Alaq 96:1 opens revelation by tying reading and learning directly to the Creator.

questions.prompt: In 96:1, reading is tied to whose name?
options: The name of your Lord who created
questions.explanation: The verse says: Read in the Name of your Lord who created.

questions.prompt: In 96:1, what is the reader first told to do?
questions.explanation: The verse begins: Read in the Name of your Lord who created.

lessons.title: The Pen & Knowledge
lessons.objective: Connect Surah al-'Alaq 96:4-5's mention of teaching by the pen with the value of knowledge and clear thinking.
lessons.hook: How does writing turn temporary ideas into a legacy that outlives a single person?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: Knowledge is a venerable estate; good manners are new dresses; and thinking is clear mirror.

lessons.summary: Surah al-'Alaq 96:4-5 highlights teaching by the pen and granting humanity knowledge it did not previously possess.
lessons.familyNote: From Nahj al-Balagha, Saying 5 (compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi, tr. Sayed Ali Reza):

questions.prompt: By what does 96:4-5 say man was taught?
questions.explanation: The verse says: who taught by the pen.

questions.prompt: What did man receive, according to 96:4-5?
questions.explanation: He was taught what he did not know.

lessons.title: The Trap of Self-Sufficiency
lessons.objective: Identify the warning against human arrogance and perceived self-sufficiency in Surah al-'Alaq 96:6-7.
lessons.hook: Why do people often become less careful about ethics right after they feel completely independent?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: Indeed man becomes rebellious when he considers himself without need.

lessons.summary: Surah al-'Alaq 96:6-7 warns that seeing oneself as self-sufficient can lead to transgression.

questions.prompt: What happens when man considers himself without need, in 96:6-7?
questions.explanation: The verse says man becomes rebellious when he considers himself without need.

questions.prompt: A team leader says, 'I do not need anyone's advice.' What does the verse warn about?
options: Seeing yourself as self-sufficient can lead to transgression
questions.explanation: The warning is against considering oneself without need.

lessons.title: Names of Mercy: al-Rahman and al-Rahim
lessons.objective: Recall how Al-Mizan Vol. 1 presents the classical distinction between al-Rahman and al-Rahim in Surah al-Fatihah 1:1.
lessons.hook: Why does the opening verse of the Qur'an use two different Arabic words derived from mercy (rahmah) side by side?

sources.book: Al-Mizan: An Exegesis of the Qur'an, Vol. 1
sources.author: Allamah Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i
sources.quote: ar-Rahman (the Beneficent) is a special name with a general attribute; and ar-Rahim (the Merciful) is a general name with a special attribute.

lessons.summary: In Al-Mizan Vol. 1, Allamah Tabataba'i notes that both al-Rahman and al-Rahim derive from al-rahmah (mercy) and quotes Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq's concise distinction between a special name with a general attribute and a general name with a special attribute.
lessons.familyNote: The quoted distinction comes directly from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, cited in Al-Mizan Vol. 1.

questions.prompt: In the quoted description, ar-Rahman is...
options: A special name with a general attribute
A general name with a special attribute
A name for the Day of Judgement
questions.explanation: ar-Rahman is described as a special name with a general attribute.

questions.prompt: In the quoted description, ar-Rahim is...
options: A special name with a general attribute
A general name with a special attribute
questions.explanation: ar-Rahim is described as a general name with a special attribute.

lessons.title: Presence in Worship (1:5)
lessons.objective: Explain Allamah Tabataba'i's insight on Surah al-Fatihah 1:5 that true worship requires conscious presence.
lessons.hook: What separates going through the motions of a routine from actually being present in it?

sources.book: Al-Mizan: An Exegesis of the Qur'an, Vol. 1
sources.author: Allamah Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i
sources.quote: The true worship, therefore, is that in which the worshipped and the worshipper both are present.

lessons.summary: Al-Mizan Vol. 1 explains that 1:5 shifts to direct address ("You") so the worshipper stands consciously present before God rather than offering an empty form.

questions.prompt: In this passage, what makes worship true?
options: Both the worshipped and the worshipper are present
questions.explanation: The quote says true worship is where both are present.

questions.prompt: Why does 1:5 shift to saying 'You'?
options: So the worshipper stands consciously present before God
questions.explanation: The summary says direct address places the worshipper before God, not offering an empty form.

lessons.title: Reading a Chapter as a Unified Whole
lessons.objective: Explain why Al-Mizan Vol. 1 treats each Qur'anic chapter as a single coherent unit with a unified aim.
lessons.hook: Why does reading one sentence out of a chapter often miss the point of the whole page?

sources.book: Al-Mizan: An Exegesis of the Qur'an, Vol. 1
sources.author: Allamah Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i
sources.quote: every chapter is a single unit in structure and in fullness of meaning

lessons.summary: Al-Mizan Vol. 1 explains that every Qur'anic chapter has its own thematic unity; in Surah al-Fatihah, the verses flow as a single arc from praise to servitude to praying for guidance.

questions.prompt: Order the three-part flow of Surah al-Fatihah described in Al-Mizan.
questions.explanation: The verses flow from praise to servitude to praying for guidance.

questions.prompt: What does the quote say about each chapter?
options: It is a single unit in structure and fullness of meaning
It is a list of separate sayings
It is unrelated to its own verses
questions.explanation: Each chapter is a single unit in structure and in fullness of meaning.

lessons.title: Readiness for Guidance (2:2-3)
lessons.objective: Identify the qualities associated with guidance at the opening of Surah al-Baqarah (2:2-3).
lessons.hook: Why can two people read the same text and walk away with completely different levels of insight?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: This is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance to the Godwary, who believe in the Unseen, maintain the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them;

lessons.summary: Surah al-Baqarah 2:2-3 introduces the Qur'an as guidance for the God-conscious, linking inner conviction with prayer and sharing what one has been provided.

questions.prompt: In 2:2-3, the Book is a guidance to whom?
questions.explanation: The verse says a guidance to the Godwary.

questions.prompt: Which three qualities does 2:3 connect with the Godwary?
options: Believing in the Unseen, maintaining prayer, spending from what was provided
questions.explanation: The verse lists belief in the Unseen, maintaining the prayer, and spending out of what has been provided.

lessons.title: Explaining the Qur'an with the Qur'an
lessons.objective: Describe Allamah Tabataba'i's core method in Al-Mizan: explaining the Qur'an with the help of the Qur'an itself.
lessons.hook: How do you keep from distorting a book when a single line seems unclear on its own?

sources.book: Al-Mizan: An Exegesis of the Qur'an, Vol. 1
sources.author: Allamah Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i
sources.quote: the author made a detailed plan to explain the Qur'an with the help of the Qur'an itself

lessons.summary: The WOFIS Foreword to Al-Mizan Vol. 1 explains that Allamah Tabataba'i built his commentary around letting related verses of the Qur'an illuminate one another rather than isolating single lines.

options: Explaining the Qur'an with the Qur'an itself
questions.explanation: The author planned to explain the Qur'an with the help of the Qur'an itself.

questions.prompt: One verse seems unclear on its own. Which approach fits?
questions.explanation: Related verses illuminate one another.

lessons.objective: Summarize Imam Ali's description of the Qur'an's three time horizons in Nahj al-Balagha Saying 313.
lessons.hook: Is the Qur'an mainly about ancient history, the future, or how to live today?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: The Qur'an contains news about the past, foretellings about the future and commandments for the present.

sources.quote: Referring to Allah means to act according to what is clear in His Book.

lessons.title: Feasible, Steady Recitation (73:20)
lessons.objective: Connect Surah al-Muzzammil 73:20 to sustainable, realistic engagement with the Qur'an.
lessons.hook: Why does consistency in small amounts usually outlast intense bursts that lead to burnout?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: So recite as much of the Quran as is feasible

lessons.summary: Surah al-Muzzammil 73:20 encourages reciting as much of the Qur'an as is feasible, grounding spiritual habits in realism rather than burnout.

questions.prompt: How much does 73:20 say to recite?
options: As much as possible in one night
questions.explanation: The verse says: recite as much of the Quran as is feasible.

questions.prompt: You have a busy schedule. Which plan fits 73:20?
options: A small amount you can keep up every day
A huge amount for a week, then stop
questions.explanation: The verse grounds the habit in what is feasible, not in burnout.

lessons.title: Living What You Recite (2:44)
lessons.objective: Reflect on aligning one's own conduct with the principles one recites and recommends to others.
lessons.hook: Why is it easier to point out what others should do than to hold ourselves to the same standard?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: Will you bid others to piety and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Do you not exercise your reason?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: Make yourself the measure (for dealings) between you and others. Thus, you should desire for others what you desire for yourself

lessons.summary: Surah al-Baqarah 2:44 questions those who urge others to righteousness while forgetting themselves despite reciting the Book.
lessons.familyNote: From Nahj al-Balagha, Letter 31 (compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi, tr. Sayed Ali Reza):

options: Urging others to piety while forgetting yourselves
questions.explanation: The verse questions bidding others to piety while forgetting yourselves.

questions.prompt: A message tells everyone how to behave, but its writer ignores the same advice. What does 2:44 ask?
options: That your own conduct match what you urge on others
That you give no advice at all
questions.explanation: The verse asks about forgetting yourselves while urging others.

lessons.title: Tier 2 Boss Checkpoint: Seeing Signs Without Forgetting the Creator
lessons.objective: Synthesize Tier 2 around Al-Mizan Vol. 1's principle that looking at creation should remind the heart of God rather than distract from Him.
lessons.hook: When you admire something remarkable in the world, does it pull your attention away from its Source or point back toward it?

sources.book: Al-Mizan: An Exegesis of the Qur'an, Vol. 1
sources.author: Allamah Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i
sources.quote: Nothing in the creation can hide the divine presence, nor should looking at these things make one forgetful of Allah.

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.quote: Is it not sufficient that your Lord is witness to all things?

lessons.summary: Al-Mizan Vol. 1 teaches that creation belongs to God and should never veil the observer from Him; every sign in the universe and within oneself points back to the Creator.
